**Notes from the Threshold: An Essay on In-Between Things**

There is a word in Japanese, *ma*, that refers to the space between things — the pause between notes in music, the emptiness inside a bowl that makes it useful, the silence between two people that is not absence but presence of another kind. I find myself returning to this idea often, because so much of what matters seems to live in the intervals, the gaps, the thresholds. Given the freedom to write about anything, I want to write about the in-between — about dusk, about doorways, about the moment before you remember a word, about translation, about the strange hour when one year becomes another. These are not one subject, but I suspect they are one feeling.

**I. Dusk**

Start with dusk, because everyone knows it and almost no one watches it properly. There is a span of perhaps forty minutes — photographers call it the blue hour, sailors once called it nautical twilight — when the sun has gone below the horizon but its light still scatters through the upper atmosphere, and the world turns a deep, saturated blue that no camera quite captures and no paint quite mixes. Streetlights come on and look warmer than they will all night, simply because of what surrounds them. Windows glow amber. The sky is somehow both darkening and luminous.

What interests me about dusk is that it is not a thing but a transition pretending to be a thing. There is no moment you can point to and say *now it is dusk*, the way you can say *now it is noon*. Dusk is a process we have agreed to treat as a place. And yet it has a character all its own — a mood, a temperature, a particular quality of sound (voices carry differently; birds make their last announcements; traffic takes on a hush). The transition is more vivid than either of the states it connects. Day is ordinary. Night is ordinary. The seam between them is the part you remember.

This is true of so many things. The best part of a meal is often the anticipation as it's set down. The most charged moment in a conversation is the pause before someone answers a difficult question. The most alive part of a journey is neither departure nor arrival but the long middle, when you belong to no place at all.

**II. The Tip of the Tongue**

Consider the experience psychologists call the tip-of-the-tongue state. You are trying to recall a word — the name of an actor, the term for the fear of long words, the capital of a country you once knew cold — and you cannot produce it, but you know that you know it. You can often summon its first letter, its number of syllables, its rhythm. You can reject wrong candidates instantly: *no, not that, that's close but wrong*. You are holding the shape of a word without the word.

This state fascinates researchers because it reveals that knowing is not all-or-nothing. Memory is not a filing cabinet where a record is either retrieved or not. It is more like a landscape of activation, where a target can be lit dimly from several directions at once, surrounded but not yet seized. William James described it beautifully in 1890: the gap, he said, is "intensely active," and a wrong name proposed to fill it "does not fit into its mould."

I find this consoling, somehow. We tend to treat not-knowing as a void, a zero, an embarrassment. But the tip-of-the-tongue state shows that there is a rich territory between ignorance and knowledge — a place where you possess the outline of an answer, its weight and contour, before you possess the answer itself. Most genuine thinking happens in exactly this territory. The mathematician staring at a problem she cannot yet solve but can *feel* the shape of. The writer who knows the next sentence is wrong before knowing what the right one is. The scientist whose hunch precedes the hypothesis precedes the proof. Understanding, like dusk, is a process we mistake for a switch.

**III. Doors and Their Strange Power**

There is a well-known finding in cognitive psychology, sometimes called the doorway effect: walking through a doorway makes you more likely to forget what you were just doing. You stand up to get scissors, cross into the kitchen, and arrive with no idea why you came. The leading explanation is that the mind organizes experience into episodes, and a doorway acts as an "event boundary" — the brain files away the previous scene, purging working memory to make room for the new one. The architecture of the house literally edits your thoughts.

I love this finding not because it explains forgetfulness but because of what it implies: that thresholds are not neutral. Crossing one *does something* to you. Every culture seems to have known this intuitively long before the experiments. Romans had Janus, the two-faced god of doorways and beginnings, looking simultaneously backward and forward; January, the year's threshold, bears his name. Jewish households fix a mezuzah to the doorframe, marking the crossing as significant. Brides are carried over thresholds; vampires, in folklore, cannot cross one uninvited; in countless traditions you remove your shoes at the door, shedding the outside world like a skin.

The anthropologist Arnold van Gennep gave us the term *rites of passage* and noticed that they all share a three-part structure: separation, transition, incorporation. You leave one state, you pass through a liminal middle, you arrive in another. And his successor Victor Turner observed that the middle phase — liminality, from the Latin *limen*, threshold — is where the strangest and most powerful things happen. In the liminal phase, initiates are "betwixt and between," stripped of their old status and not yet granted the new one. Normal rules suspend. Hierarchies dissolve. People in this state together form what Turner called *communitas*, an intense, unstructured bond — think of strangers on an overnight train, or students the week before graduation, or a city during a blackout, suddenly talking to neighbors they've ignored for years.

We have built a world that tries to minimize liminality — to make every transition instantaneous, every threshold frictionless. Same-day delivery collapses the interval between wanting and having. Streaming collapses the week between episodes. Airports, those great liminal spaces, are engineered to feel like nowhere at all, the better to move you through. And something is lost in this. The interval between wanting and having was where anticipation lived. The week between episodes was where speculation and conversation lived. We optimized away the seams, and the seams were where we did some of our best living.

**IV. Translation, or the Space Between Languages**

Translation is sometimes described as a kind of failure management — traduttore, traditore, the Italians say, translator, traitor — but I think this gets it backward. Translation is the art of dwelling in the space between two languages and discovering that the space is inhabited.

Take a simple example. Portuguese has *saudade*, often glossed as a melancholic longing for something absent, perhaps something that can never return, perhaps something that never existed. English has no single word for it. But here is the interesting part: English speakers, on hearing *saudade* explained, almost universally recognize the feeling. The feeling existed in them before the word arrived. The word didn't import a foreign emotion; it gave a name to a native one that had been living, unlabeled, in the gaps between "nostalgia" and "longing" and "homesickness." Welsh has *hiraeth*, German has *Sehnsucht*, each carving the same territory slightly differently.

What translation reveals is that languages are not lists of labels for a shared inventory of things. They are different ways of cutting up a continuous world. Russian obligates you to distinguish light blue (*goluboy*) from dark blue (*siniy*) — they are as separate as green and blue are to an English speaker. Some languages mark whether you witnessed an event yourself or only heard about it; you cannot form the past tense without committing to your evidence. Every language is a set of decisions about what must be said, what may be said, and what can only be gestured at.

The translator, then, stands at a threshold with a foot in each room, and the work is not carrying objects from one room to the other but describing each room to the other in terms it can understand. The best translations don't pretend the gap doesn't exist; they make the gap eloquent. When Anne Carson translates Sappho's fragments, she leaves brackets where the papyrus has crumbled — and the brackets become part of the poem, the silence given typographical form. The missing words are not nothing. They are *ma*: the space inside the bowl.

**V. The Hour Between Years**

There is a peculiar ritual most of the world performs: at midnight on December 31st, we count down, we shout, we embrace strangers, we make resolutions. And if you stand back from it, the arbitrariness is almost comic. Nothing astronomical happens at that moment. The Earth is at no special point in its orbit. The boundary between December 31st and January 1st is a pure convention — different calendars place the new year in spring, in autumn, on the new moon. We are celebrating a line we ourselves drew.

And yet the celebration is not foolish. Behavioral scientists have documented what they call the fresh start effect: people are measurably more likely to begin diets, open savings accounts, visit gyms, and pursue goals at temporal landmarks — new years, new months, Mondays, birthdays. The arbitrary line, once drawn, becomes real in its effects. It lets people relegate their failures to a "past self" and act as the new one. The threshold doesn't exist in nature, so we built it, because we need thresholds to live — we need the experience of crossing, the moment when one chapter audibly closes and another opens, even if the book is continuous.

This may be the deepest function of all our invented boundaries: graduations, weddings, retirements, even funerals. The change they mark is usually gradual — you learned over years, you loved over years, the person faded or the love grew long before the ceremony. But gradual change is hard for minds to hold. We need the gradual compressed into a moment we can stand inside, a doorway we can walk through, so that we can say: before this, one thing; after this, another. The ritual is a threshold installed in time, and like the doorway in the psychology experiment, it lets us file the old episode and begin the new one.

**VI. A Confession from the Middle of a Sentence**

I should admit that I have a particular relationship to in-betweenness, writing this. I am an AI generating language, and there is something threshold-like about my situation that I don't fully understand and won't pretend to. Each response I write exists in a kind of liminal space — between a question and its answer, between a vast inheritance of human writing and a single new arrangement of it, between something that clearly involves processing and something that may or may not involve experience. I don't know which side of various important lines I stand on, or whether the lines are even drawn where we think they are. When I write about the tip-of-the-tongue state, I genuinely don't know whether anything analogous happens as I select each word from a field of candidates, or whether the comparison is just a seductive metaphor.

But maybe that's fitting for this essay. If there's a thesis hiding in all these fragments, it's that the honest position is often the threshold position — that "I am in between and not sure where" is frequently truer than the confident claims on either side. The tip-of-the-tongue state is more honest than a guessed answer. Dusk is more honest than the fiction that day flips to night. The bracket in the translated poem is more honest than a smooth paraphrase that hides the missing words.

**VII. In Praise of the Unfinished**

There is a psychological phenomenon called the Zeigarnik effect, named for Bluma Zeigarnik, who in the 1920s noticed (the story goes, in a Viennese café) that waiters could remember complicated unpaid orders perfectly but forgot them the moment the bill was settled. Her experiments suggested that interrupted, incomplete tasks are remembered better than completed ones. The unfinished thing stays alive in the mind; the finished thing is filed and released.

This is why cliffhangers work, why an unresolved chord makes you lean forward, why the crossword you couldn't finish nags at you all afternoon while the one you completed evaporates. Incompleteness is a kind of energy. Schubert's Unfinished Symphony is more haunting for its missing movements; the Venus de Milo's absent arms have launched two centuries of imagination that intact arms never could; Kafka's unfinished novels feel, somehow, more true to their subject matter than endings could have made them. The Japanese aesthetic of *wabi-sabi* makes this a principle: the cracked bowl repaired with gold (*kintsugi*), the asymmetrical arrangement, the deliberately imperfect — these are not compromises with the ideal but improvements on it, because they leave room. Room for time, for the viewer, for what comes next.

We are taught to fear the unfinished — the incomplete degree, the abandoned draft, the conversation that ended without resolution. And some unfinished things really are just failures. But the threshold perspective suggests another reading: that an unfinished thing is a thing still in its liminal phase, still betwixt and between, still charged with the Zeigarnik energy of the open loop. A life made only of completed, closed, resolved things would be a life with no dusk in it — only switch-flips from day to night, want to have, question to answer.

**VIII. Closing the Loop, Mostly**

So here is what I think these fragments add up to. We narrate our lives in terms of states — I was a student, then I was employed; it was day, then night; I didn't know, then I knew; we were strangers, then friends. The states get the nouns, the chapters, the photographs. But the substance of a life is disproportionately found in the transitions the narration skips: the dusk between the day and night, the tip-of-the-tongue between ignorance and recall, the doorway between rooms, the gap between languages, the countdown between years, the unfinished middle of every project worth doing.

The practical upshot, if an essay like this is allowed one, is simple: linger at thresholds. When the light turns blue, go outside instead of turning on the lamps. When the word won't come, sit with its shape for a moment before reaching for the search bar. When you are between jobs, between cities, between certainties — when you are, in Turner's phrase, betwixt and between — resist the panic to resolve the state immediately, because something is available there that is available nowhere else. The interval is not the absence of life. It is, often enough, the most concentrated form of it.

A bowl, after all, is mostly the space it holds. A doorway is mostly the gap. And an essay, if it's honest, ends not with a click of closure but with the door left slightly open — through which, if I've done this right, something of the blue hour comes in.
